section_summary: This section traces U.S. diplomatic monitoring of Japanese and East Asian periodicals during the immediate postwar transition. It begins with correspondence about the Russian-language Japanese propaganda magazine Vostochnoe Obozrenie and a proposal for educating American foreign-origin communities, then provides extensive reviews of Japanese magazines addressing democratization, war responsibility, constitutional reform, economic reconstruction, and intellectual life. The final pages transmit and reproduce the opening portion of the first New Taiwan Monthly, an English-language publication promoting Taiwan under restored Chinese administration.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning Vostochnoe Obozrenie and Japanese Russian-language propaganda
subfiles.from: Yaroslav J. Chyz, Common Council for American Unity
subfiles.about: Chyz describes the missing Russian-language Japanese magazine Vostochnoe Obozrenie, its contributors, and its potential evidentiary value.
subfiles.summary: Chyz thanks Durbrow for seeking six issues of Vostochnoe Obozrenie he gave State in 1940-1941, calls the South Manchuria Railway publication ideological support for expansion with named contributors, recalls a 1941 Pacific-strategy article, and encloses a memorandum on foreign-origin groups in the U.S.

subfiles.title: Memorandum regarding the Common Council for American Unity
subfiles.about: Murphy assesses the Common Council for American Unity and warns that its otherwise commendable program might be exploited by Communist-aligned activists.
subfiles.summary: Murphy thinks most Common Council for American Unity board members reputable but a few linked to fellow-travelling groups, recalls Common Ground's earlier direction under Louis Adamic and Alan Cranston, alleges penetration, and urges scrutiny of who would run its educational program.

subfiles.title: American Foreign Policy and Our Foreign Origin Groups
subfiles.to: William Benton, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum proposes State Department information and consultation programs directed toward Americans of foreign birth or parentage.
subfiles.summary: Paper: millions of Americans keep strong ties to ancestral countries, causing tension when U.S. policy conflicts with those countries' aims, as with Soviet relations and Lithuania; it warns foreign-language communities may organize around concerns apart from U.S. interests and recommends translated materials and consulting their representatives.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Chyz’s letter and enclosure
subfiles.about: Durbrow acknowledges receiving Chyz’s information about Vostochnoe Obozrenie and the memorandum on foreign-origin groups.
subfiles.summary: Durbrow acknowledges Chyz's October 23 letter on the Russian-Japanese magazine and its propaganda authors and says it and the policy memorandum went to other interested officers.

subfiles.title: Correction concerning the sixth issue of Vostochnoe Obozrenie
subfiles.about: Chyz corrects his earlier recollection of articles in the sixth issue of Vostochnoe Obozrenie.
subfiles.summary: After borrowing the sixth issue, Chyz finds the Pacific-strategy article concerns U.S., not Japanese, strategy, that Admiral Soosa's article was on another subject, and that Hawaii and the Philippines appeared elsewhere; he asks Durbrow to circulate the correction.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 87: Review of Magazine New Life (Shinsei)
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The despatch introduces a review of the first two issues of the new Japanese monthly Shinsei.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 87: Atcheson reports paper and equipment shortages slowed periodicals while surviving magazines swapped militarist themes for democratic ones; Shinsei, edited by Murobuse Takanobu, is the most promising review despite his pan-Asian past; Japanese political journalism remains confused and uneven.

subfiles.title: Review of Shinsei (Vita Nova), November and December issues
subfiles.about: This enclosure summarizes political, economic, social, and constitutional articles in the first two issues of Shinsei.
subfiles.summary: The review portrays Shinsei’s inaugural issue as hastily assembled but important as the first major postwar literary review, with contributions spanning liberalism, socialism, inflation, war responsibility, and cooperative reform. Its account of the December issue emphasizes public-debt repudiation, democracy, Japanese racial psychology, Minobe Tatsukichi’s constitutional theory, and alternative models for Japan’s political economy. It also summarizes a denunciatory article naming numerous politicians and bureaucrats as collaborators with militarism.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 173: Reviews of Recent Japanese Periodicals
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards Matsuhei Matsuo’s reviews of four Japanese public-affairs magazines.
subfiles.summary: The mission transmits reviews of Gendai, Koron, Sozo, and Jimmin Hyoron. It also notes the January 1946 revival of Chuo Koron and Kaizo, formerly Japan’s foremost literary reviews, and identifies Royama Masamichi as Chuo Koron’s editor. The mission promises to forward further magazines and reviews when possible.

subfiles.title: Review of Gendai, November 1945
subfiles.about: The review surveys Gendai’s conservative postwar issue, chiefly devoted to Japan’s food crisis and economic recovery.
subfiles.summary: Review of Gendai, November 1945: conservative, centered on food supply, advocating agrarian reform, land redistribution, modernization, currency stabilization, education change and youth in politics; it includes rightist Kodama Yoshio and defends democracy's compatibility with the emperor system.

subfiles.title: Review of Koron, October 1945
subfiles.about: The review examines Koron’s first post-surrender issue and its tentative shift from nationalism toward democratic language.
subfiles.summary: Koron, formerly highly nationalistic, is said to have adopted a moderately democratic appearance after the war. Its contributors discuss American science, educational reform, a socially constrained liberalism, unemployment, food policy, agrarian redistribution, and Japan’s coming party system. Several articles nevertheless retain deference to imperial institutions and conservative assumptions.

subfiles.title: Review of Sozo, October 1945
subfiles.about: The review characterizes Sozo as a conservative magazine retaining much of its nationalist outlook.
subfiles.summary: Review of Sozo, October 1945: dominated by Satomi Kishio's defense of his wartime writing and reconciling democracy with Japan's polity, plus calls for a cultural renaissance freed from mythology and popular science; no recognized liberal contributors.

subfiles.title: Review of Jimmin Hyoron, November and December 1945
subfiles.about: The review surveys the first two issues of the leftist but formally non-Communist Jimmin Hyoron.
subfiles.summary: Review of Jimmin Hyoron: November urges repealing the Peace Preservation Law and a progressive Potsdam reading; December demands Japanese punishment of war criminals, warns against conservative control of constitutional revision, and proposes flexible food quotas; presented as the people's voice, not a Communist Party organ.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 321: Current Japanese Review Magazines
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Bishop forwards a study of the suppression, revival, and character of Japanese review magazines.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 321: wartime suppression of major reviews and slow postwar revival from shortages, with Shinsei, Jimmin Hyoron, Chuo Koron, Kaizo and Sekai reappearing; Bishop notes few young writers, little natural science and excess abstract polemics, and calls for accessible democratic reading for youth.

subfiles.title: Memorandum: Current Japanese Review Magazines
subfiles.to: Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Matsuo provides a detailed history and assessment of Japanese review magazines before, during, and after the Pacific War.
subfiles.summary: Matsuo traces how censorship, propaganda policy, bombing, paper shortages, and the suppression of Chuo Koron and Kaizo weakened serious magazines during the war. He then follows the postwar return of older reviews and the creation of Shinsei, Jimmin Hyoron, Sekai, Choryu, Hyoron, and other publications, comparing their editors, ideological tendencies, readerships, and commercial reception. The study argues that these magazines can guide the intelligentsia but suffer from an aging contributor base, neglect of natural science, and overly abstract debate. It concludes that Japan also urgently needs elementary democratic periodicals and booklets for intellectually deprived young and rural readers, and appends a list of current magazines and publishers.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 16: Transmitting Copies of the First Issue of The New Taiwan Monthly
subfiles.about: Blake transmits copies of the first New Taiwan Monthly and comments on its discussion of Taiwan’s administration under Chinese rule.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 16 sends five copies of the first New Taiwan Monthly, noting articles on Taiwan's administrative independence and waning enthusiasm for Chinese control, and that it calls Chen Yi governor, not Governor-General; copies to Nanjing and Shanghai.

subfiles.title: The New Taiwan Monthly, first issue, opening pages
subfiles.from: Stanway Cheng and the New Taiwan Publishing Co., Ltd.
subfiles.about: The opening portion of the first New Taiwan Monthly introduces the magazine and presents Taiwan’s geography, resources, liberation, and early history.
subfiles.summary: The issue contains its cover, map, contents, Ralph Blake’s endorsement, and a foreword announcing an objective English-language publication supporting China’s open-door policy and explaining Taiwan to the outside world. Articles celebrate Taiwan’s return to Chinese sovereignty after Japanese rule, credit Roosevelt, Churchill, and Chiang Kai-shek with the Cairo declaration, and promote the island’s scenery, resources, schools, and tourist attractions. A historical essay recounts early Chinese knowledge of Taiwan, European and Japanese activity, Cheng Cheng-kung’s rule, Qing administration, the opening of treaty ports, and growing foreign interest; the excerpt ends before that article is complete.
